input:
In this example, we are going to work through the calculation of the available net positive suction head, usually abbreviated to $NPSH_a$, for a pump that is drawing water up from an open tank at 101.3 kPa. The pump draws water from the open tank at atmospheric pressure, which is 101.3 kPa, and the vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature is 2.3 kPa. In addition, the static lift that the pump has to overcome is 3.6 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 1 m. The available net positive suction head is calculated using the following relationship, in which $P_{atm}$ is the atmospheric pressure, $P_v$ is the vapour pressure, $\rho$ is the density, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, $h_{lift}$ is the static lift and $h_f$ is the friction loss:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

When all of the values are substituted into this equation, the available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ comes out at 5.5 m, and it is this available head of 5.5 m that has to be used in the comparison. It is very important to remember that this available value has to be compared against the pump's required NPSH at the duty flow, which is taken from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with a suitable margin in order to avoid problems during operation.
target:
The available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ for the pump is 5.5 m. The pump draws water from an open tank, and $NPSH_a$ (m) is obtained from the atmospheric pressure $P_{atm}$ (kPa), the vapour pressure at the pumping temperature $P_v$ (kPa), the density $\rho$, the acceleration due to gravity $g$, the static lift $h_{lift}$ (m) and the suction-line friction loss $h_f$ (m) by

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

The pressure term converts the pressure margin above vapour pressure into a head of liquid; the lift and the friction loss are then subtracted from that head. The tank is open, so $P_{atm}$ is 101.3 kPa. Substitution of $P_{atm}$ = 101.3 kPa, $P_v$ = 2.3 kPa, $h_{lift}$ = 3.6 m and $h_f$ = 1 m gives $NPSH_a$ = 5.5 m. The figure is an available head at the stated conditions, and its use is a comparison. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve, and $NPSH_a$ must exceed that required value with margin; the available head establishes nothing on its own until the required value from the vendor curve is set against it. Each term in the equation is a head, so the result is read directly against the required head, with no conversion standing between the two sides of the comparison, and the margin is the difference between the two heads at the duty flow.
